1 31번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
Studies indicate that, by around the age of three, children already grasp that imaginary objects cannot come to life. This is especially evident with everyday objects — a child knows that even if they picture a pencil inside an empty box, the box will stay empty. However, emotion can sometimes disrupt this understanding, or at least the way it is expressed. That is, even though a child knows monsters are not real, the thought of a monster under the bed can be enough to make the child refuse to enter the room at night. Indeed, research shows that children have a harder time displaying their understanding of the causal relations between imagination and reality when they are asked to imagine frightening things, such as monsters. In one study, preschool children were shown an empty box and asked to imagine a monster inside it. All the children agreed that the box was empty. However, when they were left alone with the box, they exhibited fear and avoidance of it.
①how emotion can interfere with children's grasp of imagination and reality
②how children gradually lose their ability to imagine as they age
③the cognitive stages through which children learn to read and write
④why imaginary friends are essential to early childhood development
⑤the role of parents in reducing children's nighttime fears
2 32번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
One of the best-known outcomes of broadening aesthetic experience is what we now call the aesthetics of everyday life. Although scholarship on everyday aesthetics is flourishing today, the idea that ordinary objects and events can give aesthetic satisfaction is far from new. Poets, especially the Romantics and many in Asian traditions, long prized the beauty of everyday situations, and novelists noticed it too. Its modern intellectual roots, however, are most easily traced to John Dewey's Art as Experience. There Dewey grounded aesthetic experience in the biological and cultural conditions of human life rather than treating art as something set apart. He placed the aesthetic not in private sensation but in a full meeting of the self with the world of objects and events. For Dewey, the aesthetic was simply the heightened, clarified form of features found in any complete experience.
①Dewey's grounding of the aesthetic in ordinary, lived experience
②the decline of Romantic poetry in modern aesthetic theory
③why philosophers rejected the study of everyday objects
④the technical methods novelists use to describe beauty
⑤the separation of Asian and Western aesthetic traditions

주장찾기
3 31번 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
By the age of three, most children clearly recognize that things they only imagine cannot turn into real objects. We should not, however, treat this recognition as something that always holds firm, since feelings can quietly weaken it. When a child is asked to picture something frightening, like a monster, fear can take over what the child rationally understands. For this reason, anyone trying to judge how children reason must weigh the emotional situation rather than relying on neutral tasks alone. A child who calmly says a box is empty may still refuse to stay beside it once a monster has been imagined inside. What the child knows and what the child does can therefore split apart. The behavior, not the stated belief, reveals where fear has taken control. Adults who ignore this gap risk misreading what children actually understand.
①Children should be encouraged to confront their fears on their own.
②Adults must consider emotional context when interpreting children's reasoning.
③Imagination training should begin well before the age of three.
④Frightening stories should never be told to preschool children.
⑤Parents ought to remove every imagined threat from a child's room.
4 32번 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
The aesthetics of everyday life is perhaps the most familiar result of opening up what counts as aesthetic experience. We should not assume that beauty belongs only to fine art set apart from daily living. Long before today's research, poets and novelists already found aesthetic value in ordinary moments. John Dewey gave this intuition its clearest modern footing in Art as Experience. He insisted that the aesthetic grows out of the biological and cultural conditions of ordinary human life. Rather than isolating art, we should recognize the aesthetic as part of every complete experience. To treat art as separate from life, Dewey implies, is to misunderstand what the aesthetic really is. We ought, therefore, to look for the aesthetic within everyday experience, not apart from it.
①Art should be preserved in museums to protect its value.
②Only trained critics can judge what counts as beautiful.
③The aesthetic should be recognized within everyday life, not set apart from it.
④Romantic poetry is the highest form of aesthetic expression.
⑤Philosophical theory must define beauty before artists create.

5 31번 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
Children as young as three already understand that imagined things remain imagined and cannot act upon the real world. Yet this understanding does not always reveal itself in the way they behave. Once fear is involved, a child may treat an imagined threat as if it were real while still insisting that it is not. So, under the pressure of emotion, what a child knows and how a child acts can pull in opposite directions. A preschooler shown an empty box, for example, may agree it is empty and yet avoid it after imagining a monster inside. The gap between knowledge and behavior widens precisely when the imagined content is frightening. This is why neutral tasks may overstate how steadily children apply what they know. Emotion, in short, can override reason in a young child's actions.

Expanding the idea of aesthetic experience gave rise to the now-familiar field of everyday aesthetics. The notion that ordinary things can be aesthetically rewarding is old, even if mainstream philosophy once dismissed it. Romantic and Asian poets, along with novelists, had already valued beauty in daily life. Dewey's Art as Experience offers the clearest modern starting point for this view. He tied the aesthetic to the biological and cultural conditions of human living. Beauty, for Dewey, lies in the self's full engagement with the world, not in inner sensation alone. The aesthetic is thus a heightened version of what any complete experience already contains. In short, art and life are not separate realms but deeply intertwined.

Three-year-olds reliably understand that imaginary objects never come to life, above all in ordinary, everyday situations. This rational grasp, however, can be unsettled by emotion — fear most of all. A child who firmly states that a box is empty may nonetheless refuse to remain near it after being told to imagine a monster inside. Knowledge, it turns out, does not always prevail over feeling. When children are asked to picture something scary, they show their understanding less consistently than with neutral content. In experiments, preschoolers agree an empty box is empty, yet display fear once left alone with it. Their actions, more than their words, reveal the pull of emotion. The lesson is that a young child's certainty can dissolve the moment fear enters.

Further, Dewey maintained that the aesthetic is the clarified and intensified development of traits that belong to every normally complete experience.
Dewey (A) aesthetic experience in the conditions of human life, opposing the (B) of art from life.

Perhaps the best-known development to emerge from the liberation and expansion of aesthetic experience is the aesthetics of everyday life. Although there is presently a flowering of work on everyday aesthetics, the possibility of aesthetic gratification in ordinary objects and events has long been recognized, even if degraded and dismissed by prevalent philosophical theory. Widely valued by poets, especially Romantic poets and those in Asian traditions, the aesthetic in everyday situations has also been recognized by novelists. It may be most convenient, though, to locate its contemporary intellectual origins in John Dewey's Art as Experience. In that book Dewey argued against the separation of art from life by basing aesthetic experience on the biological and cultural conditions of human life. He located the aesthetic, not in an internalized awareness of sensation and feeling but in a complete interpenetration of self and the world of objects and events. Further, Dewey maintained that the aesthetic is the clarified and intensified development of traits that belong to every normally complete experience.
